en: (1.1.1) (1.1) Now, regarding the canopy:
the *brahmán*, who is learned in the *Brahmaveda*, sits to the south according to the rule, remaining silent.
(1.1.2) (1.2) He recites the consecratory formulas over the oblations that have been prescribed.
(1.1.3) (1.3) Regarding the non-instruction of mantras, Bhāgali says they should be used according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*);
Yuvan Kauśika says [the mantra] "O Prajāpati, none other than you... [RV 7.85(80).3].
"According to the respective deity," says Māṭhara;
"with *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janad o3m*," say the teachers.
(1.1.4) (1.4) Some insert the mantras for the principal oblations before the preliminary and concluding oblations.
(1.1.5) (1.5) He causes the sacrificer to recite [the formula] consecrated by one who knows the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras verses.
(1.1.6) (1.6) The Āhavanīya fire is Agni.
(1.1.7) (1.7) Moving about and restraining speech belong to the sacrificer, just as [the duties] belonging to the Brahman priest do.
(1.1.8) (1.8) The deities, the oblations, and the sacrificial fees [are derived] from the Yajurveda.
(1.1.9) (1.9) The approach is from the north of the Āgnīdhra;
[he approaches] while standing facing south, with the *sphya* and the means of purification (*saṃmārga*) in his hands.
(1.1.10) (1.10) The response to the call for assent (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*) is "Let it be so, *śrauṣaṭ*," uttered according to the respective accent.
(1.1.11) (1.11) On the day before the new moon, the sacrificer, intending to fast, eats food in the afternoon.
(1.1.12) (1.12) At the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dakṣiṇa fires,
he places fuel-sticks upon them in their respective divisions with the verse, "O Agni, grant me luster" (5.3.1).
(1.1.13) He undertakes a vow with the mantra:
"O Lord of Vows, through this vow... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.78[74].4), beginning with the practice of fasting and so forth. (1.1.14) (1.14)
With the four verses beginning "O Agni, may splendor be mine" (TS 5.3.1–4), he encompasses the deities;
[with the verse] "O Sinīvālī, broad-tressed one... (TS 7.48[46]).
Thus [is the offering] with the mantra as stated;
on the full moon day, [it is performed] with the mantra "anv adya naḥ."
(1.1.16) (1.16) Having offered the morning *agnihotra* with the verse,
"The goddess *Kuhū*" [7.49(47)],
and with the verse, "That which the gods... [7.84(79)].
Thus, on the new moon day:
"I [invoke] Rākā" (7.50[48]);
"Full in the west" (7.85[80]).
Thus [it is performed] on the full moon day.
(1.1.17) (1.17) Then he chooses the Brahman priest with the formula:
"O lord of the earth, O lord of the world, O lord of the worlds, O lord of the great being, we choose you as our Brahman" (TB 3.7.6.1).
(1.1.18) (1.18) Having been chosen, he mutters:
"I am the lord of the earth; I am the lord of the world."
I am the lord of the earths;
I am the lord of the great being. That I declare to the mind, the mind to speech, speech to the Gāyatrī, the Gāyatrī to the Uṣṇih, and the Uṣṇih to the Anuṣṭubh.
The Anuṣṭubh to the Bṛhatī, the Bṛhatī to the Paṅkti, the Paṅkti to the Triṣṭubh, the Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī, the Jagatī to Prajāpati,
and Prajāpati to the All-Gods. (Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janad oṃ.)
And thus [is] the Apratiratha hymn.
(1.1.19) (1.19) Beginning with "Having sipped water with the *jīvābhiḥ* [mantras]" and ending with the act of surrender (*prapadana*).

(1.1.20) (1.20) From the north of the fire and the south of the two other fires, having entered and looked at the seat, he recites from "O Daidhiṣavya" [TS 3.2.4.4] and so forth, up to the gazing at heaven and earth.
(1.2.1) (2.1) Where one discerns [the thought], "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters," there lead forward the sacrifice; do thou cause the deities to increase.

May the sacrificer abide on the back of the firmament, in the heavenly world, where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is located; there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer.
"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janad oṃ praṇaya"— with these words, he gives permission according to the proper accents.
In this same manner, the word for permission is used at the beginning and end in all cases.
(1.2.2) (2.2) While the *praṇītā* waters are being brought forward, he restrains his speech until the *haviṣkṛt* calls for the lifting of the oblation.
(1.2.3) (2.3) If he should speak [untruth], he should mutter a Vaiṣṇava [mantra].
(1.2.4) (2.4) The Āgnīdhra, having placed the *anvāhārya* rice on the fire and having swept around the altar, sets it down in the region of the *utkara*.
Once the second layer of loose earth (*purīṣa*) for the *stambayajus* has been thrown down, he supports it with the formula:
"O Araru, do not fly up to heaven! (VSM 1.26). (1.2.5) (2.5)
With the mantra, "O Bṛhaspati, encompass it" (*bṛhaspate parigṛhāṇa*), he consecrates the altar as it is being enclosed. (1.2.6) (2.6) [He recites:
"Aspiring for goodwill" (*āśāsānā saumanasam*). (14.1.42)
Thus he addresses his wife as she is being girded.
(1.2.7) (2.7) "The clarified butter is yours, O Agni... (TS 7.87.6)—thus he addresses Agni while the clarified butter is being poured out.
To one who is strewing around the altar with the words, "Strew around" (*pari stṛṇīhi*), [he should say], "On which trees... (*yasyāṃ vṛkṣāḥ*).
Thus for the enclosing-sticks as they are being placed; (with the formula:
"Thou art the strew of the seers" for the prastara-bunch.
(1.2.10) (2.10) When the sacrificial oblations have been placed, he offers the previously mentioned *pūrva-homas* (pre-offerings);
in the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), he offers the malevolent offerings and the *saṃsthita-homas* (concluding offerings). (1.2.11) (2.11) [The mantra:
"I reflect upon Agni... [4.23]
Thus he consecrates the *sāmidhenī* verses. (1.2.12) (2.12) With the mantra, "O Prajāpati, none other than you [possesses] these...
(TS 3.4.10.3), he performs the *prājāpatya* libation. (1.2.13) (2.13)

"O Agnīdh, cleanse the enclosing-sticks and the fire three times each!"—thus he gives the command; the Āgnīdhra [cleanses] the wooden sword (sphya) and the fire. [Caland, *Altindisches Ritual*, suggests *agniṃ ca*: "and the fire."
Having performed the sweeping in between, he sweeps the middle, southern, and northern enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) three times each with the formula:
"O Agni, winner of the prize, I sweep you, the winner of the prize, as you are about to run for the prize" (*VSM* 2.7).
By means of the sweeping, he fans the fire towards himself.
"O Agni, I cleanse you who are about to win and about to gain the prize; win the prize! (cf. BaudhŚS 1.15:23.2, etc.).
With the mantra "Indra, this... (6.5.2), he performs the Āghāra libation for Indra.

(1.2.15) While the *pravara* is being chosen, he should cause [the bridegroom] to recite the three verses beginning with "The gods, the fathers... (RV 10.123.3–5). (1.2.16) [He should also recite] "Summer, winter... (RV 10.55.2).
Thus for the *prayāja* offerings. (1.2.17) (2.17) "I have brought forth" (6.61.3)—thus for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. (1.3.1) (3.1)
"Yenendrāya" (1.9.3) is dedicated to Agni;
"Mā vaniṃ mā vācam" (5.7.6).
Thus [ends] the offering to Indra and Agni.
(1.3.3) (3.3) Of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, [one recites] either the verse for Indra or that for Mahendra: "Indra,
protect this [sacrifice]" (6.5.2) and "Thou art Indra, thou art Mahendra" (17.1.18).

(1.3.4) (3.4) On the full moon day, the offerings to Agni and to Agni-Soma are performed, with the Upāṃśuyāja in between; [the offering] to Agni-Soma is for him [to obtain] sovereignty (*kṣatra*), according to [the mantra] "asmai kṣatram" (TS 6.5.4.2). This is because there is no such injunction for the new moon day. (1.3.5) (3.5)
With the verse beginning "ā devānām" (RV 10.2.3), he offers the oblation for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
(1.3.6) (3.6) After the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, once the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been performed, he restrains his speech until the impulse for the *anuyāja* offerings.
(1.3.7) (3.7) The *prāśitra* portion, the size of a barley grain, having been anointed with clarified butter either below or above, the Adhvaryu carries it around by the front.
"I gaze upon you with the eye of the sun" [PS 20.57.11,
KauśS 91.2].
[He] awaits [the command with the words: "GB 2.1.2"]. (1.3.9) (3.9) [With the words:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, being impelled by the command, I receive [thee]" (KauśS 2.2, VSM 2.11), he receives it.
(1.3.10) (3.10) Having spread out blades of grass upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he places [the staff] there with its handle pointing eastward, saying:
"I set thee on the navel of the earth" (VSM 2.11). (1.3.11) (3.11) [He places it] with:
"With the mouth of Agni" (PS 20.57.14).
With the mantra, "Thou art the self; O self, do not harm my self, svāhā" (KauśS 65.14),
he consumes [the substance] with his ring finger and thumb, without touching it with his teeth.

(1.3.12) (3.12) He consecrates the *prāśitra* portion with the mantra: "The fire named Nṛmaṇas that has entered into the Brāhmaṇas—may this *prāśitra* be well-offered into it; may it not harm me in the highest heaven" (PS 20.57.15, KauśS 65.15).
(1.3.13) (3.13) Having sprinkled himself with water from the *mārjālīya* pit, he touches his vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
(1.3.14) Having sipped water with [the mantra]:

"May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils; may sight be in my eyes; may hearing be in my ears; may strength be in my arms; may vigor be in my thighs; may speed be in my calves; may stability be in my feet."
"May all my limbs be free from harm; may my body be united with my body," [he says] over the navel. "May Iḍā herself [protect] us... [7.28(27)]
Thus he recites the mantra over the *iḍā* as it is being invoked.
(1.3.16) (3.16) The Āgnīdhra eats the sixfold portion with the formula:
"I eat you by the gift of the earth; I eat you by the gift of the atmosphere; I eat you by the gift of heaven" [MānŚS 1.3.3.16]. (1.3.17) (3.17) "May the god [approach] you... [7.115(110)].
Having accepted the portion of the *iḍā* with [the mantra] "indra gīrbhiḥ" (7.115[110].3cd), they consume it with [the mantra] "itīḍābhāgaṃ pratigṛhya" (7.115[110].3ab).
With the three verses beginning with "apo divyāḥ" (7.94[89].1–3), they perform the purification over the strainers.

(1.3.19) (3.19) The sacrificer [places] the *anvāhārya* rice within the altar (*vedi*). (1.3.20) (3.20) "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati; full of vigor, full of milk; thou art imperishable; for imperishability I take thee. Mayest thou not perish for me, both there in that world and here."
Protect my prāṇa and apāna; protect my samāna and vyāna; protect my form as udāna.
You are strength; bestow strength upon me.
Do not fail me while I am acting; do not deceive me while I am giving.
Having consecrated it with the mantra, "May I, as Prajāpati, prosper through you in your presence" (GB 2.1.7), he gives the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests.
(1.3.21) (3.21) Having accepted [it], it was said:
"Who is this? [3.29.7].
(1.3.22) (3.22) Having been given the command, the Āgnīdhra [performs his duty].
Having placed a fuel-stick with the verse, "Thou art fuel" (*edho 'si*), he cleans each of the enclosing sticks once with the formula:
"O Agni, winner of booty, I cleanse thee who hast run for the prize and who art the conqueror of booty" (*agne vājavid vājaṃ tvā sasṛvāṃsaṃ vājajitaṃ saṃmārjmi*).
(1.4.2) (4.2) And he sweeps the fire toward the east with the formula: "O Agni, I sweep thee, the winner of booty; thou hast won the booty" [cf. BaudhŚS 1.19:28.2].
(1.4.3) (4.3) "May the light of the mind enjoy the clarified butter; may Bṛhaspati extend this unimpaired sacrifice; may all the gods rejoice here. [cf. AVPariś 22.9.4]
[With the verse] "TS 1.5.3.2 etc. [he offers] the *anuyāja* oblations.
(1.4.4) (4.4) [With the verse] "ye devā divi ṣṭha" [TS 1.30.3] [he offers] the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. (1.4.5) (4.5)

He recites the mantra, "Drive away, O Kāma" (*nudasya kāma*), as the two *sruva*-ladles are being pushed apart; he recites "The sacrificial grass is anointed" (*saṃ barhir aktam*) [at the appropriate time].
"Thus [he recites] as the *prastara* grass-bundle is being thrown into the fire. (1.4.7) (4.7) "'The portions of the residue'—[this is for] the residue.
"May heat not burn thee" (7.19.2);
"him with splendor" (6.53.3);
"the wives of the gods" (9.7.6).
[With the verse] "sugārhapatya" (ŚB 12.2.45cd),
he performs the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
(1.4.7) (4.7) [The offerings] into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; the third [is performed with the mantra]: "In the mortar, in the pestle" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 10.9.26).
(1.4.10) (4.10) The Āgnīdhra throws the cleansing-broom into the fire with [the mantra]:
"O Agni... (TS 7.92[87].1). (1.4.11) (4.11) [He recites: "I loosen for thee... (TS 7.83[78]).
With the verses, "I loosen you" (ŚB 14.1.57) and "I release you" (ŚB 14.1.19), he consecrates the wife as she is being released from the girdle. (1.4.12) (4.12)
With the words, "The Veda is well-being," he unties the Veda-bundle.
(1.4.13) (4.13) He offers the *saṃsthitahoma* oblations with six verses beginning with "Those whom you have brought hither" (*yān āvahaḥ*) and "O Lord of the Mind" (*manasaspate*).
Thus, among these, this is the best.
(1.4.14) (4.14) He recites the consecratory formula over the *praṇītā* waters as they are being released:
"The flowing ones... (6.23).
"Those for whom there are fore-offerings" (1.30.4)—with these words he invokes blessings upon the sacrificer. (1.4.16) (4.16) "Whatever food... (6.71).
Having thus consumed the portion, [he says]:
"O God Savitṛ, this has been declared to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice."
"Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; protect the sacrifice,
protect the lord of the sacrifice, protect me, protect me as one skilled in ritual action"— thus he says.
(1.4.17) (4.17) When the sacrificer has water poured into his joined palms, he wipes his face with the verse, "United with splendor" (RV 6.53.3).
(1.4.18) Between the two fires, to the south of the fire, he performs the rites beginning with the Viṣṇu-strides and ending with the consecration. (1.4.19) (With the verse:
"O Agni, lord of the house... [entire verse as in KauśS 70.9, cf.
VSM 2.27, etc. he worships the Gārhapatya fire. (1.4.20) (4.20)
Having approached the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "Upon whose thighs...
(RV 7.26.3), he recites, "In-breath and out-breath... (ŚB 2.16).
"Ojas tvam asi" (2.17), it is said. (1.4.21) (4.21) Having performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) with the two verses beginning "Ayaṃ no agniḥ" (entirely from KauśS 89.13; PS 20.61.5–6),...
"May the lord of the sacrifice [attain] his desire" (VSM 6.10, etc.), with these words he consumes the portion. (1.4.22) (4.22) "The vows to the Lord of Vows... (the entire text as in KauśS 42.17).
[He] offers [the oblation] with [the verse] "PS 19.51.4" as the concluding rite for the vows.
(1.4.23) (4.23) Without this [section] concerning the sacrificer, there is no accomplishment.
Regarding that, two verses state:
"The Pravargya, the duties of the sacrificer, and the mantras for the wife—these three [are required]."
Moreover, it becomes a constituent part of the sacrifice, and without these [constituents], the sacrifice fails to be accomplished.
"Through the Pravargya rite one obtains heroism, and through the Yājyā-mantras, the blessings;
through the mantras for the wife, offspring and long life; therefore, it is perfected by that alone. Thus [it is said].
(1.4.24) (4.24) The New and Full Moon sacrifices consist of thirty syllables;
the Dākṣāyaṇayajña consists of fifteen.
(1.4.25) (4.25) On the full moon day, one performs the Full Moon sacrifice, and on the following day as well;
likewise on the new moon day.
Or for one year. (1.4.26) (4.26)
(1.4.27) (4.27) And the Sākaṃprasthāyya and other sacrifices are explained by these two; they are explained.
(2.1.1) (5.1) Now, the establishment of the sacred fires.
(2.1.2) (5.2) For a Brāhmaṇa, it is in spring; for a Rājanya, in summer;
for a Vaiśya, in the rainy season.
It has been stated: "There are three joints" (KauśS 94.7).
(2.1.3) (5.3) Whenever one should offer it, faith indeed must not abandon him.
(2.1.4) (5.4) The *brahmaudana* has been explained.
(2.1.5) (5.5) He causes the officiating priests to take their seats.
(2.1.6) Or he should place [the wood] that has been consecrated with mantras. (2.1.7) "The Aśvattha tree which has grown from the womb of the Śamī, having ascended together with you—
that I take for you with the sacred word (*brahman*), along with the sacrificial signs."

While he is taking the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) as prescribed by the mantra: "O Jātavedas, pour here that seed of the world which shall be born from fervor (*tapas*); generating Agni, the bearer of oblations, from the *aśvattha* tree and from the womb of the *śamī* tree—he who is the source of bliss"—he causes the one about to establish the fires to recite it.
(2.1.8) (5.8) Restraining their speech, they remain awake during the night,
or during the latter part of the night. (2.1.9) (5.9) [Bṛhaspate savitaḥ 7.16.1]
Thus one should awaken those who are sleeping.

(2.1.10) (5.10) At dawn, he prepares the water for pacification with the *Atharvaṇa* hymns beginning with "cityā," those containing "kapūrvi," "parvā," "rodākā," "vṛkkāvatī," "nāḍā," and "nirdahantī," as well as the *Āṅgirasa* hymns, the *Cātana* rites, the *Mātṛnāman* mantras, and the *Vāstoṣpati* mantras joined [with these].
(2.1.11) (5.11) By means of that, while bathing and sprinkling the horse at the fire-place, he pacifies it.

(2.1.12) (5.12) Whether before sunrise or after sunrise, one who is about to offer [the oblation] performs the rite beginning with "ākṛtiloṣṭa" and ending with the worship (upasthāna). (2.1.13) (5.13) [The verse] "yat tvā kruddhāḥ" [12.2.5].
Thus the teachers extract [the portion] up to the marking of the Āhavanīya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires: "Thou art the earthen one, the sustainer of all. (2.1.14) (5.14) (purīṣyo 'si viśvabharāḥ).
Atharvan was the first to churn you forth, O Agni.
From the lotus, O Agni, Atharvan churned you forth from the head of the entire universe, you the worshipper.
The seer Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, kindled you,
the slayer of Vṛtra and the shatterer of forts.
"O you, the Pāthya bull, he has kindled you, the greatest slayer of Dasyus,
the winner of wealth in every battle"—
with these words, he consecrates the fire as it is being churned.
(2.1.15) (5.15) "The one who has been born, the well-born Jātavedas" (RV 4.23.4).
(2.1.36) (5.36) Having covered it with gold,
[one should recite] with the nasal *uṣman* or with the mouth:
"In me, at the beginning" (mayy agra).
Thus, by this [verse], one exhales.
(2.1.17) (5.17) While the horse's hoof is being placed upon the mark,
he recites the mantra over it: *sam adhvarāya* [3.16.6].

(2.1.18) (5.18) While the horse is being led toward the fire in a chariot, [the Adhvaryu] makes him recite [the verse] while holding onto it: (2.2.1) (6.1) "When you first neighed as you were being born, rising from the ocean or from the mound of earth—
with the wings of a falcon and the forelegs of an antelope— great and worthy of praise was your birth, O steed."

When you, O steed, were born in the waters, crying out—powerful, swift, and mighty in strength—they established you as a portion for the Brahman: O Agni, the Atharvans, the Sāmaveda, and the Yajus formulas.
Prajāpati led the horse, purified by the Ṛg-verses, first to Atharvan; in its footprint he established the first light. May it carry me to where the world of the doers of good deeds is.
Trample those who attack me; bestow offspring and long life upon me, O powerful one!
Through you may I slay my hateful rivals; grant the heavenly world to my sacrificer.
"Overpower those who attack; subdue those who fight against you, so that I may overcome all those people who seek to harm me. (The *pratīka* is found in GB 1.2.18.)
(2.2.2) (6.2) As the Āhavanīya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires are being carried forth together from the Gārhapatya fire, he recites the consecratory formula: "I separate them" (vyākaromi). (ŚB 12.2.32) //
(2.2.3) (6.3) Having established the Āhavanīya fire,
he worships it with the verse: "This cow has come" (Āyaṃ gauḥ 6.31.1–3).
(2.2.4) (6.4) The Dakṣiṇāgni is either produced by friction or brought from elsewhere.
(2.2.5) (6.5) The ritual arrangement proceeds from the Āhavanīya fire to the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires; or [it may proceed] from the Sabhya to the Āvasathya.
The Sabhya is for the assembly hall (*sabhā*).
The domestic fire for the household.

(2.2.6) (6.6) He gives the horse, the chariot, the *cātuṣprāśya* gold, and the fire-vessel to the Brahman priest. (2.2.7) (6.7) "They call you Agni Vaiśvānara; burning from your seat, you have indeed gone forth.
As such, speak for us among the gods; may we not come to harm through you. [PS 1.95.3]
Having thus pacified the horse with the verse "sakala" (also at GB 1.2.21) and the verse "yad akrandaḥ" (VaitS 6.1), [he proceeds].
Thus he performs the *upākaraṇa* ceremony.
[O blazing one, you have come; O blazing one, you have gone. (2.2.8) (6.8) [The vigor of Indra, the vanguard of the Maruts] (6.125.3).
Having thus offered oblations to the chariot, he mounts it with the verse: "O Lord of the Forest, with strong limbs... (RV 6.125.1).
(2.2.9) (6.9) Having sat down, he performs the *pūrṇahoma* with the verse:
"Upa tvā namasā" [3.15.7–8]. (2.2.10) (6.10) [He recites: "Idam ugrāya" [7.109.1].
Having spoken thus, he hands over the dice that have been cast for the purpose of gambling to the Adhvaryu.

(2.2.11) (6.11) In the *iṣṭis* pertaining to the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnyādheya*), [the verses] for Agni are: "of Pavamāna, Pāvaka, Śuci, and Aditi" (with the mantras): "May Pavamāna purify [6.19.2]" and "The brilliant one is thine [18.4.59]."
"Agni [drives away] the Rakṣases" (TS 8.3.26) and "Aditi is the sky" (TS 7.6.1).

[5.7.7] thus regarding the recitation of what is not to be praised. (3.2.11) (12.11)
With the verse "aśmanvatī" (RV 10.53.8),
one crosses over the waters; with the verse "apaḥ samudrāt" (RV 4.27.4).
Thus, for being rained upon while uncovered; (3.2.13) (12.13) "ava jyām iva" [6.42.1] for anger.

(3.2.14) (12.14) Having cooked a meal for his wife when she has reached her season, using a cow with a calf of the same color, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, removed it from the fire, taken it out, and uttered the *abhihiṃkāra* over it, he should cause her to eat it after it has been mixed with the remnants of the *garbhavedana* and *puṃsavana* rites.
(3.3.1) (13.1) There are three initiation days, or an unlimited number.
The twelve-day [rite] belongs to the Ahīna sacrifice.
(3.3.2) (13.2) At the end of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), at the *prāyaṇīyā* offering, [he offers] to Pathyā Svasti, Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, and Aditi, with the verses: "The wealthy paths...
(3.4.7) and "The Veda is well-being" (7.28.1).
(3.3.3) (13.3) They conclude with the *śaṃyu*-formula.
(3.3.4) (13.4) For Dhruva, the full-offering is with the verse: "In whose broad [thighs]...
(3.3.5) (13.5) Having gone out, he consecrates the Soma-purchase cow as she is being led forward with the mantra: "Ascend to heaven" (TS 1.3.4.3).
(3.3.6) (13.6) The offering at the footprint (*padābhihoma*) is performed with the verse beginning "The footprint of Iḍā" (*iḍāyās padam*, 3.10.6).
(3.3.7) (13.7) At the place of the *uparava* holes, with his hands covered in gold, he sorts the *soma* upon the hide while reciting, "Toward that one... (*abhi tyam* [RV 7.14.1]). (3.3.8) (13.8)
He consecrates [the water] with the mantra: "This is a thousand" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.2.1).
(3.3.9) (13.9) Once the purchase has been made, he removes the *kurīra* head-net.
(3.3.10) (13.10) He rises with the words, "Up with life! (*ud āyuṣā*).
(3.3.11) (13.11) While it is being carried forward, he mutters the *Apratiratha* hymn.
(3.3.12) (13.12) With the words, "The firm with the firm" (*dhruvaṃ dhruveṇa*), he consecrates the King as he is being led from the royal litter onto the throne-seat.

(3.3.13) (13.13) Having caused [the guest] to stand to the south of the fire, they touch the sacrificial oblation of the *ātithyā* ceremony with the mantra: "By sacrifice, sacrifice [is offered]" (TS 7.5.1).
(3.3.14) (13.14) The Vaiṣṇava [hymn] is "viṣṇor nu kam" (RV 7.26.1).
(3.3.15) (13.15) It ends with the *iḍā*.
(3.3.16) (13.16) They cut off the clarified butter five times into the *tānūnaptra* vessel, saying:

"I take thee for the lord of the fallen; I take thee for the lord of those around; I take thee for the grandson of the body; I take thee for the powerful one; I take thee for the mightiest of the strong" (TS 1.2.10.2, etc.). [GB, G: he cuts off.]
(3.3.17) (13.17) They touch it:
(3.3.18) (13.18) "Unassailable, unassailable by others, the vigor of the gods, protecting from imprecation, beyond imprecation.
May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration; may the Lord of Penance approve my penance."
"May I straightway attain truth; place me in well-being"—thus the initiated one possesses the characteristic mark of initiation.
(3.3.19) (13.19) The Adhvaryu says to the Āgnīdhra:
"Āgnīdh, the waters are bubbling! (agnīt madantyāpā3ḥ).
(3.3.20) (13.20) The Āgnīdhra [recites]:
"The divine waters rejoice, immortal, increasing the cosmic order."
(3.3.21) (13.21) The Adhvaryu [says]: "Rise up with them."
(3.3.22) (13.22) The Āgnīdhra leads them up with *kuśa* grass.
(3.3.23) (13.23) Having touched them, they cause the Soma to swell:
"O divine Soma, may each stalk of thine swell for Indra, the winner of the single prize;
may Indra swell for thee, and mayest thou swell for Indra."
"May you cause us, your friends, to swell with gain, with wisdom, with offspring, and with wealth.
May it be well with you, O divine Soma; may I attain the conclusion of the pressing."
(3.3.24) (13.24) Having touched water again, with their hands turned upward, they make a silent confession upon the sacrificial grass (*prastara*) with the formula:
"Desired are riches; desired are blessings; for the impulse, for fortune; to the *ṛta* and to those who speak the *ṛta*, obeisance to heaven, obeisance to earth" [TS 1.2.11.1, GB 2.2.4].
(3.3.25) (13.25) Having offered the preliminary oblations for the Pravargya, he sits down to the south of the Gārhapatya fire.
(3.3.26) (13.26) One should not perform the *pravargya* rite at one's first sacrifice;
however, one who is learned in the Vedas and a *śrotriya* may do so at will.
(3.3.27) (13.27) Having stepped aside, the Adhvaryu says:
"O Brahman, we shall proceed with the *gharma*. [GB 2.2.6]
(3.3.28) (13.28) He gives permission with the words, "Proceed with the Gharma.
(3.3.29) (13.29) Everything is recited either loudly or in a whisper.
(3.3.30) (13.30) One should worship the *gharma* while it is being heated. (3.4.1) (14.1) "I heat the *gharma* with a stream of nectar, as an offering to the gods, a gift for Savitṛ.
O gods, let them eat the bright, cooked oblation; let them consume what is offered with the *juhū*-ladle in the womb of immortality."
The Lord of the gods comes; the Gharma, shining by the *ṛta*, beholds immortality.
Golden-hued, O divine Sūrya, you, the Gharma, shining with lightning, traverse the ends of heaven from the sky.
Vaiśvānara goes around the ocean, the bright *gharma* shining and radiant with splendor;
driving away my enemies and burning up my rivals, the wise Āditya has ascended to heaven.
It shines forth, it glows, and it shines within the waters—the immortal Gharma rising up.
The slayer of Vṛtra, the host of the bay horses, the unassailable bodies of the Sun.
The Gharma is behind, and the Gharma is in front; we hurl it against the foe with its iron teeth.
May Vaiśvānara, clothed in cold and heat, slay all my rivals who hate me.
With the seasons he cooks through the seasons; the Gharma, the sole hero by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), being heated and kindled with fuel.
Brahman illumines you with Brahman and with splendor.
The thousandfold heat, kindled with fuel—
may the quarters be free from rivals for me;
may Sūrya Vaiśvānara, the golden-hued, destroy all my rivals.
May the heated Gharma burn away my rivals;
may the bull Āditya, rising as the bright Sūrya, slay those who hate me and my adversaries.

(PS 16.152.5–7) [The verses] beginning with *brahma jajñānam* (4.1.1) and *iyaṃ pitryā* (4.1.2) are recited verse by half, like a *śastra*, excluding the calls (*āhāva*) and responses (*pratigara*). (3.4.2) (14.2)
With the words, "Thou art pleasing" (TS 1.1.21), he consecrates that which has been approved.
(3.4.3) (14.3) "The two who milk the Gharma rise to milk it" (*uttiṣṭhatāva paśyata* 7.72.1).
Thus [is the verse] for the Gharma-milking cow.
(3.4.5) (14.5) With the *gharma-sūkta*, while the *gharma* is being offered,
he recites the two verses beginning with "svāhākṛtaḥ" (7.73.3–4) at the *vaṣaṭ*-call and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*-call for the *gharma*.
(3.4.6) (14.6) The consumption [of the offering] is like that of the *vājina*:

"May we eat of thee, O Gharma, the cooked oblation, the honeyed oblation—honeyed, accompanied by the ancestors, possessed of strength (*vāja*), accompanied by Bṛhaspati, and belonging to all the gods."
(3.4.7) (14.7) In a sacrificial session (*sattra*), there are the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, their respective assistants, and the Gṛhapati.
(3.4.8) (14.8) They purify themselves over the remains on the donkey with strainers.
(3.4.9) (14.9) When the verse beginning with *sūyavasaḥ* (RV 7.73.11) has been recited three times, they perform the concluding oblations.
(3.5.1) (15.1) Having approached [the fires], [he offers oblations] to Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu.
(3.5.2) (15.2) [The formulas for] the replenishing and the concealment end with the *vaṣaṭ* call.

(3.5.3) (15.3) When the Adhvaryu says, "O Āgnīdhra, announce the wives of the gods," then the Āgnīdhra, standing behind the Gārhapatya fire facing eastward, announces the wives of the gods without pausing for breath.
Earth is the wife of Agni; Speech is the wife of Vāta; Senā is the wife of Indra; Dhenā is the wife of Bṛhaspati;
Pathyā is the wife of Pūṣan; Gāyatrī is the wife of the Vasus; Triṣṭubh is the wife of the Rudras;
Jagatī is the wife of the Ādityas; Anuṣṭubh is the wife of Mitra; Virāj is the wife of Varuṇa; Paṅkti is the wife of Viṣṇu; and Dīkṣā is the wife of Soma.
"The king's wife" (GB 2.2.9, TA 3.9.1).
(3.5.4) (15.4) At the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā, in all cases, he mutters three verses beginning with "In which [the Sadas]... (ŚB 12.1.38–40).
(3.5.5) (15.5) Thus, on the afternoon [of the first day], the *gharma* and *upasad* rites are performed;
on the following day, both in the forenoon and the afternoon;
and on the *aupavasathya* day, they are completed together.
(3.5.6) (15.6) Thus there are three for the Agniṣṭoma; twelve for the Ahīna. (3.5.7) (15.7) "Measure out! [13.1.27]
With the words, "Thus he measures the altar," he consecrates the altar as it is being measured.
With the words, "On which altar... he consecrates the altar as it is being enclosed.
(3.5.9) (15.9) While the fire is being led forward, having murmured "O Agni, go forth" [4.14.5], he sits down outside the sacrificial altar.
(3.5.10) (15.10) Over the path of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he performs an offering with the verse, "This Viṣṇu... (*idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, 7.26.4).
For the northern one, [he does the same].
"Three steps" (trīṇi padā).
(3.5.11) (15.11) While the *havirdhāna* shedder is being set in motion,
he consecrates it with two verses beginning with "From here and from there" (*itaś ca mā*). (3.5.12) (15.12)
"Viṣṇor nu kam" (7.26.1)—
with this, the supporting pillar is being supported. "Manve vāṃ dyāvāpṛthivī" (4.26.1).
Thus ends the libation over the Audumbarī post.
(3.5.14) (15.14) Having been addressed for the purpose of leading forward Agni and Soma, he enters the wife’s hall by way of the *tīrtha*.
The *tīrtha* consists of the space between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap, as well as the area north of the mark of the *āgnīdhrīya* shed and the *sadas* hall.

(3.5.15) (15.15) [The rites] beginning with the sipping of water (*ācamana*) and ending with the looking (*vīkṣaṇa*). (3.5.16) (15.16) With the half-verse, "Soma the King" [RV 3.20.4ab], he follows after Agni and Soma as they are being led forth.
(3.5.17) (15.17) After the oblation at the Āgnīdhrīya fire, he passes behind the fire to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya and sits down on the seat.
(3.5.18) (15.18) Now, the ritual rules have been stated regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma; by this, the [rules for] other animal sacrifices are explained.
(3.5.19) (15.19) It ends with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
(3.6.1) (16.1) While the *vasatīvarī* waters are being carried around,
he follows them with the mantra: "O woman, bring the full [vessel]" (3.12.8).
While being placed on the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar, they are addressed with the following verse:
"amūryāḥ" (1.4.2).
(3.6.3) (16.3) The initiated one dwells there.
(3.6.4) (16.4) In the latter part of the night, the officiating priests, having been awakened, touch water at the door of the sacrificial hall.

(3.6.5) (16.5) With the verses beginning with *havir upāvṛtaḥ* and ending with *vaiśvānaro ’gniṣṭomaḥ*, which constitute the limbs of the sacrifice (*yajñatanū*), he offers oblations on the Āgnīdhrīya fire before the performance begins. (3.6.6) (16.6) And according to the rule *yajūṃṣi yajñe* [5.26], in the case of a competitive contest, he offers with four verses each before the *prātaranuvāka*.
(3.6.7) (16.7) Having passed behind the Āhavanīya fire to the south, he sits down as the Āsādaka.
(3.6.8) (16.8) When the Hotṛ has sat down, having offered the oblation with the verse, "That which through forgetfulness...
(*yad asmṛti*, Ṛgveda 7.106), he performs the *purastāddhoma* offerings. (3.6.9) (16.9)
He mutters four hymns after the Prātaranuvāka: *pātaṃ na indrāpūṣaṇā* (6.3–6), and *ambayo yanti* (1.4–6). (3.6.10) (16.10)
Thus there are three verses addressed to Aponaptrīya. (3.6.11) (16.11) With the verse "O Indra, enjoy!
[2.5], he offers the Abhiṣavaṇa oblations while the King [Soma] is being pressed.
The offering of the *upāṃśu* cup is performed at sunrise with the verse: "Sūrya [has risen] to the sky" (ŚB 13.1.4.5).
And this [is] the Antaryāma cup.

(3.6.12) (16.12) Having passed by the east of the *havirdhāna* shed and having sat down upon the *khara* mound, he takes recourse with the King [Soma] using the *Madhusūkta*, beginning with the verse: "From heaven, from earth... (RV 1.90.1). (3.6.13) (16.13)
He consecrates the Soma contained in the *droṇakalaśa* with the mantra: "O priests, [offer] the Soma to Indra" (Ṛgveda 6.2), and [recites]:
"Drink boldly" (Ṛgveda 7.76.2).
Thus [it is stated] in the Mādhyandina [recension].
(3.6.15) (16.15) Where [he] perceives that "O Brahmin, the Soma has spilled," he touches that [spot] with this [verse] and consecrates it with the mantra.

"Savitṛ, the god worthy of praise, has arisen; he is now to be invoked by men at this time of day—he who distributes treasures to human beings. May he grant us here the most excellent wealth" (ṚV 4.54.1). "The fires that are within the waters... (GB 2.2.12) (3.6.16) (16.16) (3.21.1–7).
Thus he offers seven oblations.

(3.6.17) (16.17) The Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Prastotṛ, the Udgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the Brahmā, having pressed the Soma and being joined together by touch, having moved out for the Bahiṣpavamāna chant, offer the Vaipruṣa oblations with the verse: "The drop has fallen" (RV 1.91.20; PS 20.13.7).
Whatever drop of yours falls away, whatever stalk of yours has been shaken from the arms, from the lap of the *dhiṣaṇā*,
or from the strainer of the *adhvaryu*— that I offer for you with my mind, consecrated by the cry of *vaṣaṭ*.
May this divine Bṛhaspati pour together for the sake of prosperity that drop which has fallen from the horse, even beyond the ladles.
That drop of yours which has fallen upon the earth— the parched grain, the Soma, the husks, and the groats—
may this divine Bṛhaspati pour it back together for you, for the sake of splendor.
[As it is said: "That which has been spilled by me... (PS 20.13.8–10). (The mantra *yan me skannam* is found in the *Kauśika Sūtra* 6.1, but is not attested elsewhere.)
(3.7.1) (17.1) They sit down to the south of the *cātvāla* pit. (3.7.2) (17.2) Reciting the mantra, "O Night, sing! (*doṣo gāya*), he gazes at the *udgātṛ*.
(3.7.3) (17.3) After the commencement of the chant, the Prastotṛ addresses the Brahman, saying:
"O Brahman, we shall chant; O Praśāstṛ!"
"Thou art a ray; for habitation thee, quicken habitation! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati!"
O God Savitṛ, he has declared this to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice. Sing forth the long-lived Ṛc and the body-protecting Sāman.
May your blessings be true; may your intentions be true.
"Speak *ṛta* and *satya*. O Bṛhaspati, with the approval of Anumati, *oṃ bhūr janad indravantaḥ*. Having said this, [he should] praise.
Thus he gives the impulse with the first tone-measure at the morning pressing,
with the middle one at the midday pressing,
and with the highest one at the third pressing. (3.7.5) (17.5)
"Bhuvaḥ" at the midday pressing;
"Svar" at the third pressing.
(3.7.6) (17.6) In the Ukthya and other sacrifices, as well as in the Ahīna, [the formulas are]: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," "janad vṛdhat," "karad ruhan," "mahat," "tac cham," and "oṃ."
(3.7.7) (17.7) While the two [sacrificers] are competing and have both purchased the *soma*, [the chanters] should chant over and over the *stomabhāga* verses:

"Praise! Praise for strength! Praise! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ—Bṛhaspati for you, Prajāpati for you, the Vasus for you, O gods; the Rudras for you, O gods; the Ādityas for you, O gods; the Sādhyas for you, O gods; the Āpyas for you, O gods; the Viśve Devas for you, O gods; all the gods for you!"
"From all sides we invoke you;
may he be ours alone among all people; from here let him perform his heroic deed"—reciting this, he should look at the *brahman* priest of the opponents.
The hymn for the hymned is full of vigor, full of milk;
may the hymn yield vigor for me. May the hymn of the hymned come to me.
We invoke those possessed of power; may we milk forth offspring and nourishment.
"May this true blessing of mine be among the gods; may it lead me to spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," with these words he consecrates the *stotra*. (3.7.9) (17.9)
"Indrasya kukṣiḥ" (7.111.1) [is recited] when the Soma has been poured into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel.
(3.7.10) (17.10) During the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite:
"Thou art a falcon" (6.48.1); "Thou art a bull" (6.48.3).
Thus at the midday pressing;
"Thou art Ṛbhu" (Ṛgveda 1.111.2) at the third pressing.
(3.7.11) (17.11) "Those spoken by the Brāhmaṇas" refers to the Anubrāhmaṇins.
(3.7.12) (17.12) Then the Adhvaryu says: "O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes."
(3.8.1) (18.1) At the Āgnīdhra fire, the Āgnīdhra priest distributes embers for two pressings;
for the third pressing, he uses wooden sticks.
Facing west, he distributes them upon the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*) of the Hotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Acchāvāka, as well as on the Mārjālīya mound.
(3.8.2) (18.2) He brings it back to that very same place.

(3.8.3) (18.3) Having spread [the grass] along the spine, he adorns the sacrificial cakes. (3.8.4) (18.4) "The fires which have been distributed as hearths across the earth—may they protect us, may they favor us; homage to them! May they not harm us."
Thus he consecrates those who have been dismissed;
at the two subsequent pressings, he uses [the verse]: "May power come back to me again" (RV 7.67.1).
It has been stated [that one should sit] behind the Āhavanīya fire.

(3.8.5) (18.5) Those engaged in ritual activity offer the *pravṛta* oblations with [the formula]: "May I be dear to Speech; may I be dear to the Lord of Speech. O Goddess Speech, place me in that which is the sweetest part of speech.
Svāhā! To Speech, svāhā! To the Lord of Speech, svāhā! To Sarasvatī, svāhā!"
With the mind, the fourth [offering]. (GB 2.2.17) (3.8.6) (18.6) "There are seven oblations," say some:
"To Sarasvatī, svāhā! To the great ones, to the thoroughly great ones, svāhā!"
"With a Ṛc, [one praises] the Stoma. Thus it is said.
(3.8.7) (18.7) Having stood up at the end of the wiping of the omentum, they worship the sun with the verse: "On the back of heaven" (ŚB 13.2.37). (3.8.8) (18.8)
Having returned with the words, "May we not go astray" (*mā pra gāma*), he addresses the Āhavanīya fire, the fire produced by friction, the sacrificial post, and the sun:
"O fires, you are the Sagaras; by your name Sagara and by your fierce aspect, protect me! O fires, fill me; O fires, guard me! Homage be to you! Do not harm me! (*namo vo 'stu mā mā hiṃsiṣṭa*).
(3.8.9) (18.9) They proceed northward from the Āgnīdhrīya fire-hall toward the Sadas.
(3.8.10) (18.10) Those possessing their respective hearths (*dhiṣṇya*) and the sacrificer proceed by the eastern door; the others [proceed] by the western door.
(3.8.11) (18.11) Those about to step forward into the *sadas* pay homage to the *dhiṣṇya* hearths with the words:
"Homage, homage to the *dhiṣṇyas*" (cf. GB 2.2.18). (3.8.12) (18.12) [They also say:
"Homage to the Seer" (ĀpŚS 12.20.6).
[They approach] the seer with the mantra, "20.1.17 etc.";
[they approach] the eavesdropper with the mantra, "Homage to the eavesdropper" (ĀpŚS 24.11.2). [Cf. GB 2.2.19].

(3.8.13) (18.13) They pay homage to the *cātvāla*, the *utkara*, the *śāmitra*, the slaughter-cow, the two *āhavanīya* fires, the *āgnīdhrīya*, the *ācchāvākavāda*, the *mārjālīya*, the *khara*, and the other *dhiṣṇya* hearths with the formula:
"O fires, you are full of moisture" (*agnayaḥ sagarā stha*; cf. above). (3.8.14) (18.14) "Go through the wide mid-region" (*urv antarikṣaṃ vīhi*; ĀpŚS 6.8.6).
Thus they touch the Sadas. With the formula, "O divine doors, do not cause me to suffer; O you two makers of space, create space for me," they touch the two door-posts.
(3.8.15) (18.15) Having crept forward, [he addresses] the Anukhyātṛ with the formula: "Homage to the Anukhyātṛ" [ĀpŚS 20.1.17, etc.].
Having circumambulated the sacrificial hearths (*dhiṣṇya*) by the north, they have each crept toward their own respective hearth;
[he addresses] the supervisor (*upadraṣṭṛ*) with: "Homage to the supervisor! (*upadraṣṭre namaḥ*).
(3.8.16) (18.16) Having sat down, they mutter the hymn "Abhi tvā indra" [RV 6.99.1];
the sacrificer recites the stotra.
(3.8.17) (18.17) The Sadasya [stands] to the south of the Brahman;
[he performs] the mental recitation of the *stotrānumantraṇa* with the mantra "janat."
(3.8.18) (18.18) When [the fires] have been rearranged according to their hearths, those who possess hearths exit by the northern door through the eastern one;
[they pass] by the Maitrāvaruṇa hearth.
(3.9.1) (19.1) The sacrificial cakes for the *savanīya* offerings belong to Indra.
(3.9.2) (19.2) Of the cups for two deities:
the two offerings of the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*) [are performed with the formula] "Vāyu [is the lord] of the intermediate space" (*vāyur antarikṣasya*). (5.24.8)
"Indra and Vāyu" (Ṛgveda 3.20.6).
(3.9.3) (19.3) For the Maitrāvaruṇa: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, [you are] of the rain" (RV 5.24.5).
(3.9.4) (19.4) For the Āśvina cup, [one uses] the half-verse: "O Aśvins, with the sacred word... (RV 5.26.12ab).
(3.9.5) As they set out, intending to perform the rite, the Adhvaryu issues the command:
"O Hotṛ, sacrifice! O Praśāstṛ, O Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, O Potṛ, O Neṣṭṛ, O Agnīdh! (cf. ĀpŚS 12.23.16, 12.24.1). (3.9.6) [The Hotṛ recites:
"O Indra, we [invoke] you, the bull... (20.1.1).
Thus the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin performs the sacrifice;
the Potṛ and the Āgnīdhra perform with the following two [verses].

(3.9.7) (19.7) The *yājyā* verses float [with protracted vowels] at their end. (3.9.8) (19.8) For those beginning with "ye yajāmahe" and ending with "vauṣaṭ," both the beginning and the end have protracted vowels (*ādipluta*).
(3.9.9) (19.9) Without taking breath at the morning pressing, having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call: "Speech, vigor, power; vigor, power, vital breath and out-breath in me" [VSM 36.1].
He consecrates [the offering] with the mantra, "O Agni, partake of the Soma" (GB 2.3.6).
They perform the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* with a protracted final syllable: "O Agni, partake of the Soma! (ĀpŚS 19.3.1; GB 2.3.1).
(3.9.11) (19.11) For the libations from the *śukrāmanthin* cups dedicated to Indra,
[the verse is] "Indra from heaven" (*indro divaḥ*, Ṛgveda 5.24.11).
(3.9.12) (19.12) For the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*s: "Come to the gods" (*ā devānām*); and also for the *anuhoma*s.
The [cup] for Mitra and Varuṇa, the one for Indra, the one for the Maruts, the one for Tvaṣṭṛ, and the one for Agni.
(3.9.13) (19.13) When the Agnīdh has offered, the Adhvaryu says: "The Agnīdh has sacrificed" (*ayāḍ agnīt*); the Agnīdh responds: "He has sacrificed" (*ayāṭ*).
(3.9.14) (19.14) The consumption of the *iḍā* portion is as previously described.
(3.9.15) (19.15) Having been invited, they consume the Soma draughts in the assembly hall.
(3.9.16) (19.16) Having looked at it as for the *prāśitra* portion and having received it: "Of the moon that has been offered in the fire, drunk by Indra, possessed of power—
of that which is the food bestowing cattle, bestowing horses, bestowing wealth, bestowing progeny, and bestowing worlds."
"Of that which has been invited, I, being invited, eat with the Gāyatrī metre, with splendor, and with the luster of a Brāhmaṇa."
(3.9.17) (19.17) "With the *traiṣṭubha* [meter]" refers to the midday pressing; "with the *jāgata* [meter]" refers to the third pressing;
"with the *anuṣṭup* meter" refers to the ritual sequences (*paryāya*).
With the verse "paṅkticchandasā," [one offers] in the *saṃdhicamasas*;
with "aticchandasā" in the *aptoryāma*.
(3.9.18) (19.18) Having consumed [the Soma], they touch themselves:
"O Soma, be auspicious to our heart when drunk; like a father to his son, O Indra, be very kind to us.
Like a friend to a friend, O wise one of wide renown, prolong our life-span, O Soma, that we may live."
"Stir my limbs, O Lord of Bay Horses; do not let my troops be scattered.
Be auspicious to me as you attend the Seven Seers; let not my voice pass below the navel. (TS 3.2.5.3) Thus.
(3.9.19) (19.19) They cause the cups to swell with the [mantras]: "Swell up; may your milks... [entirely as in KauśS 68.10, possibly PS 20.55.4+6].

Regarding this, there is a verse: "The sage should cause the five cups themselves to swell in the sacrifice—at the *ājya* and the *marutvatīya*, and also for all those that have been set forth. (3.9.20) (19.20)
(3.9.21) (19.21) The offering from the *acchāvāka* cup is dedicated to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*).
(3.9.22) (19.22) If they eat at the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
(3.9.23) (19.23) Seated in the *sadasya* hall, they sacrifice to the seasons according to the *praisha* calls.
(3.10.1) (20.1) With the first and last [verses] beginning with "The Maruts from the office of the *potṛ*" (20.2.1), the *potṛ* [performs the sacrifice].
By the second [verse], the Āgnīdhra;
by the third, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
(3.10.2) (20.2) The sacrificer gives the *atipraiṣa* command:
"O Hotṛ, sacrifice this! [ĀpŚS 12.27.6, etc.]
(3.10.3) (20.3) They do not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.

Regarding this, there is a verse: "The cups for the two deities, the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyāja*), the cup for Pātnīvata, the Āditya cup, and the Sāvitra cup—do not pronounce the *anuvaṣaṭ* for these. (BaudhŚS 25.20:252.4, etc.)
[Regarding the statement: "These two [libations] do not have the *anuvaṣaṭ* call" (3.10.5).

[The offerings are]: the seasonal oblations (*ṛtuhoma*); those for Indra, the Maruts, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Agni; those for Indra, Mitra-Varuṇa, and four for the Draviṇodas; and those for the Aśvins and the Gārhapatya fire.
(3.10.6) (20.6) They consume [the remnant] from the *ṛtu*-cup, or they smear it [on their lips], or they smell it, saying:
"Who art thou? Thou art glory; thou art the giver of glory; bestow glory upon me."
(3.10.7) Having silently received the *nārāśaṃsa* cups, they consume them with the formula:

"O divine Soma, who art drunk by Narāśaṃsa, praised by men, the knower of the mind, consumed by our ancestral fathers, being invited, I, invited, consume thee" (cf. AB 7.34, PB 1.5.9). (3.10.8) (20.8)
"With the thighs" at the midday [libation];
"with the poetic insights."
Thus at the third pressing. (3.10.9) (20.9) With the mantra, "Now we summon the mind" (*mano nv ā hvāmahi*), they invoke the mind.
(3.10.10) (20.10) They consume the Nārāśaṃsa cups five times.

Regarding this, there is a verse: "One should consume the five *camasa* cups at the *nārāśaṃsa* offerings; [one should consume] those which belong to the Hotṛ's earlier recitations prior to the *āgnimāruta*. (3.10.11) (20.11)
(3.10.12) (20.12) From the *ājya* recitation, the [offering] belongs to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*).
(3.10.13) (20.13) He gives the impulse for the *prauga* stotra for the Hotṛ:
"Thou art the advance; for the sake of the sacred law (*dharman*), quicken the sacred law" (PB 1.9.2, TS 4.4.1.1, cf. GB 2.2.13).
For the Maitrāvaruṇa...
"You are the connection; for heaven, you; quicken heaven.
For the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin: "You are the junction; for the intermediate space, you; quicken the intermediate space."
"To the Acchāvāka; you are a support; for the earth, you; quicken the earth. (PB 1.9.5, TS 4.4.1.1)
(3.10.14) (20.14) After the *prauga* recitation, there is the *vaiśvadeva* [śastra];
for the Maitrāvaruṇa, the *maitrāvaruṇa*;
for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the *aindra*.
The offering for the Acchāvāka priest is dedicated to Indra and Agni.
The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, having uttered *hiṅ* three times after the final *pratīhāra*, calls out to the Adhvaryu with the words, "Śaṃsāvaḥ! (Recite, let us two!).
(3.10.16) (20.16) [One should recite] without the *hiṅkāra* for the *anurūpa*, the *ukthamukha*, the *paridhānīyā*,
and the *pragātha* at the midday pressing.
(3.10.17) (20.17) Some [use] the *yonis*.
(3.10.18) (20.18) For the *stotriya*, [the formula is]: "O Adhvaryu, recite! Śaṃsāvaum! (GB 2.4.4).
"At the third pressing, [the call is]: 'O Adhvaryu, recite! Śaṃsāvoṃ! (GB 2.3.10).
(3.10.19) (20.19) At the *āhāva* calls, the Adhvaryu responds with the formula: "Let us two recite for the gods" (*śaṃsāvo daiva*). (3.10.20) (20.20)
"Om, thus, O God! at the conclusion; "Om, thus, O God!"
Thus at the *praṇava*;
"Om" at the end of the *śastra*.
(3.10.21) (20.21) He utters the response to the *uktha*:
"When the *ukthas* have been completed:
*om ukthaśā ukthaśā yaja ukthaśāḥ*. (cf. GB 2.3.10)
He continues the *śastra* with the *sāman* verse by half-verses, using a low voice at the morning pressing, and with a stronger voice at the midday pressing.
At the third pressing, he should exert himself with the strongest effort, increasing his vigor further and further until the completion [of the rite]. (3.11.1) (21.1) (Recite:
"Come hither, for we have well pressed [the Soma] for thee. (20.3)
"Come to us who have pressed the soma" (*ā no yāhi sutāvataḥ*)—
these are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses. "This one,
O you who observe all people" (*ayam u tvā vicarṣaṇe*).
Thus ends the opening of the *uktha*; "Lift up the well-known evil" (*uddhed abhi śrutām agham*) is the *paryāsa*.
The final verse is the concluding verse.
He recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times.
(3.11.4) (21.4) In the case of recitation by half-verses (*ardharcaśas*), one connects the end of the verse with the *praṇava*, having removed the initial vowel;
in the case of recitation by quarters (*pacchaḥśasya*), one connects the end of the half-verse.
At the end of the *śastra*, one connects [the final syllable] with the *makāra* alone.
Having recited [the hymn], he says:
"The hymn has been spoken for Indra" (GB 2.3.10, etc.).
Thus at the midday pressing;
"The hymn has been spoken for Indra and the gods" at the third pressing.
(3.11.6) (21.6) The perfection of the Ukthya:
the verse following the *paridhānīyā* is the *yājyā*.
(3.11.7) (21.7) From the portion of the Acchāvāka:
"Agni at the morning pressing" (6.47.1);
"Thou art a falcon" (6.48.1).
"Just as Soma at the morning pressing" (9.1.11)— with these words, he offers the clarified butter according to each pressing.
(3.11.8) (21.8) [The rules for] the concluding oblations.
At each conclusion of a *savana*, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite:
"In me be splendor, in me greatness, in me glory, in me all."
(3.11.10) (21.10) Having been dispatched for the midday pressing, they go out by the western door toward the Udumbara post and creep from the Āgnīdhrīya shed;
the sacrificer goes by the eastern door.
(3.11.11) (21.11) [He performs] the offerings before [the main sacrifice].
(3.11.12) (21.12) The pressing and so forth have been explained.
(3.11.13) (21.13) They proceed to the seat for Pavamāna.
(3.11.14) (21.14) Being addressed, he gives the impulse: "Thou art the support; for rain thee; quicken the rain" (PB 1.9.6, TS 4.4.1.1, cf. GB 2.2.13).
(3.11.15) (21.15) During the procession, if he goes outside while the *dhiṣṇya* hearths are present, he approaches a *dhiṣṇya* and mutters:
"Around thee, O Agni... (*pari tvāgne* [RV 7.71.1]).
And Brahmā as well.
(3.11.17) (21.17) When the consecrated one is outside the sacrificial ground, at the time of the *abhyāśrāvaṇa* call, or at sunset or sunrise, he says:
"O fires, come hither! (3.11.18) (21.18) "I consider it cooked" (*śrātaṃ manye*). [Ṛgveda 7.72.3]
Thus concludes the oblation of the curd-heat (*dadhigharma*).
(3.11.19) (21.19) The consumption [of the offering] is like that of the *gharma*, by means of tasting the essence.
(3.11.20) (21.20) For the sacrificial cake of the animal sacrifice: (3.11.21) (21.21) "Thus protect us...
(*evā pāhi*)—these are the *prasthitayājyā* verses.
The Prasthita oblations dedicated to Indra.
At the *gārhapatya* fire, the two *dākṣiṇa* oblations are performed with the verses: "Upwards that [sun]...
(*ud u tyam*) and "The bright [face] of the gods... (*citraṃ devānām*).
(3.11.24) (21.24) With golden hands, the sacrificer stands up outside the sacrificial altar as the sacrificial gifts arrive, reciting: "The cows have come" (RV 4.21.1).
He gives gold to the Ātreya;
he gives a pillow to the Āgnīdhra.

(3.11.26) (21.26) To the east of the *gārhapatya* fire and to the west of the *sadas*, between the *āgnīdhrīya* and the *sadas*, and between the *sadas* and the *cātvāla* pit, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*) are released toward the north.
He consecrates them with two verses: "May he unite you... (3.14.2–3). (3.12.1) (22.1)
Bhāgali says: "In which [the word] *pūrve* occurs, [as in] *bhūtakṛtaḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.39);
[and also] "*ihed asātha*" (Pāṇini 3.8.4).
Thus says Kauśika.
(3.12.2) (22.2) Finally, it should be given to the *pratihartṛ*.
(3.12.3) (22.3) The oblation for Marutvat:
"May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, [protect me]" (TS 1.8.25).
(3.12.4) (22.4) From the *śastrayājyā*, he gives the impulse (*prasauti*) to the *hotṛ* and the others: "O impeller, for the day thee; quicken the day!"

"You are the Anuvāsī; for the night, you; quicken the night! You are the Uśij; for the Vasus, you; quicken the Vasus! You are the Praketa; for the Rudras, you; quicken the Rudras! (cf. PB 1.9.8, TS 3.5.2.3, GB 2.2.13).
(3.12.5) (22.5) For the Niṣkevalya [śastra], the Māhendra [cup].
(3.12.6) (22.6) For the *praśāstṛ* and others, there is the offering to Indra.
(3.12.7) (22.7) "Him, your wondrous one, who overcomes the attackers" (20.9.2);
"That heroic power of yours, I implore of you" (20.9.3).
Thus are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses.
(3.12.8) (22.8) He recites two or three verses by taking them up again.

Having recited the first verse, he repeats its last quarter-verse (*pāda*) and, having concluded it, recites the second verse with the second half-verse (*ardharca*). Having repeated the last quarter-verse of that [second verse], he recites the third verse with the following half-verse.
(3.12.9) (22.9) Thus is the interweaving (*pragrathana*) of the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses belonging to the *bṛhatī* meters.
(3.12.10) (22.10) These two [hymns] should be recited with a voice that is neither too low nor too high.
(3.12.11) (22.11) The *sāmapragātha*, "ud u tye madhumattamāḥ" [RV 1.47.1], should be recited with a melodic tone (*svaravatī*). (3.12.12) (22.12)
"Indra, the breaker of forts, has overcome [them]"—this opening of the *uktha* is recited foot by foot with the most distinct enunciation:
"Upward have risen the sacred hymns, seeking glory... (RV 1.81.1).
Thus is the reversal. He concludes with the verse, "Even thus Indra... (RV 20.12.6).
He sacrifices with the highest [verse].
(3.12.15) (22.15) From the portion of the Acchāvāka, he performs the oblation of the Āditya cup with two verses beginning: "O gods, whatever offense against the gods... [RV 7.89.5–6].
The Pavamāna [laud] ends with the sarpaṇa.
(3.12.16) (22.16) As the *āśira* is being poured into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel, he consecrates it with the mantra: "The milk-mixture [is] strength for the one who has mixed" (Āśīrṇa ūrjam).
(3.12.17) (22.17) He gives the impulse for the Pavamāna [offering] with [the formula]: "Thou art good offspring;
for the Ādityas, thee! Quicken the Ādityas" (PB 1.9.11, GB 2.2.1). (3.12.18) (22.18) [This is] the offering of the portion belonging to Agni.
(3.12.19) (22.19) At the Ukthya sacrifice, [the offering] is dedicated to Indra and Agni; at the Ṣoḍaśin, it is dedicated to Indra; at the Atirātra, it is dedicated to Sarasvatī.
(3.12.20) (22.20) In the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice involving animals, there are offerings to Agni, Soma, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, the Viśvedevas, Indra, Indra-Agni, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa.
(3.12.21) (22.21) This begins with the *savanīya* oblation and so forth.
[The mantra: "O Indra and Bṛhaspati, drink the Soma... (20.13.2–3).
Thus are the *yājyās* for the offerings:
those for Indra, Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra-Bṛhaspati, the Maruts, Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra-Viṣṇu, and Agni.

(3.12.22) (22.22) In the *havirdhāna* shed, according to their respective goblets, they place three cakes each—prepared from the remnants of the sacrificial offerings—on the south side for their own seats, saying: "This for thee, O great-grandfather" (*etat te pratatāmaha*). (3.12.23) (22.23)
Having murmured here, "O Pitṛs... [as in KauśS 88.18, cf. VSM 2.31, ManB 2.3.6, etc.], he...
This portion;
(these are our companions);
the falcon, beholding men.
Thus he recites the consecratory formula.
(3.13.1) (23.1) They consume the remains of the sacrificial oblation at the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
(3.13.2) (23.2) The offering of the Sāvitra draughts.
(3.13.3) (23.3) [The verse] for the Vaiśvadeva offering: "With these, O Agni... (aibhir agne [20.13.4]), following the oblations to the Dhiṣṇya fires.
Thus the Āgnīdhra sacrifices for the Pātnīvata cup in a whisper.
(3.13.4) (23.4) His oblation.
Seated on the lap of the Neṣṭṛ at the edge of his hearth, he consumes [the portion].
(3.13.6) (23.6) He gives the impulse to the Hotṛ for the Agniṣṭoma-sāman with:
"Thou art vigor; for the fathers, thee; quicken the fathers" (PB 1.9.12, TS 3.5.2.3, GB 2.2.13).
(3.13.7) (23.7) "The firm one with the firm one" (RV 7.94.1).
Thus he recites the mantra over the fire as it is being established firmly.

It has been stated that when the Āgnīdhra is thus prompted with the call, "Recite for this beautiful sacrifice... (*prati tyaṃ cārum adhvaram*), he performs the offering of the *yājyā* verses for the Āgnimāruta deities.
(3.13.9) (23.9) The *hāriyojana* oblation with the verse beginning,
"With the low-sounding ones" (*ā mandraiḥ*, Ṛgveda 7.117.1).
By that very same [path], they emerge.
At the Āgnīdhrīya fire, he offers the oblations pertaining to all expiations.
(3.13.12) (23.12) All [should offer] the *śākalas* into the fire:
"Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods, svāhā! [Thou art the expiation] for the sin committed against the ancestors!"
That which is done by humans;
that which is done by oneself;
and that which is done by one who has not yet understood what is to be known.

"O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed with our tongue or through the negligence of our minds—O Vasus, lay that sin upon him who is hostile toward us and seeks to bring us misfortune" (RV 10.37.12). Thus [it is said]. (TS 3.2.5.7, PB 1.6.10)
And with the two hymns for the offense against the gods.
(3.13.13) (23.13) Having taken roasted grains from the *droṇakalaśa* vessel with their hands, they scatter them upon the ashes.
(3.13.14) (23.14) To the west of the *cātvāla* pit, the Adhvaryu pours out the water-cups containing Soma that have been set down, with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu:
(3.13.15) (23.15) "Both the young sages, the bestowers of truth from the foundation of the Law—by the foundation of the Law of Truth, we dissolve our bonds of friendship. [ĀpŚS 13.18.2, etc.]
Thus they release the friendships;
with "We unite the friendships," they unite them during a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*) prior to the final day.
(3.13.17) (23.17) They consume the curds at the Āgnīdhrīya fire with the verse, "Of Dadhikrāvan... (RV 4.39.6).
After the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, he sits down at the *śālāmukhīya* fire.
(3.13.19) (23.19) Having passed behind the Āhavanīya fire by the path for the movement of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), he offers the *saṃsthitahoma* oblations following the *samiṣṭayajus*.
In the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, one recites "In the waters, O you...
(*apsu te*) before the *pūrvahomas*.
The *sāvitra* oblations are performed with the verses "saṃsthita-homa," and the *vāruṇa* oblation with the two verses "tvaṃ no agne" (3.20.5) and "sa tvaṃ naḥ" (20.46.3).
(3.13.21) (23.21) Some [hold that] the offerings end with the *iḍā* and the *anuyāja*s.
(3.13.22) (23.22) He makes offerings with drops mixed with curds, reciting:
"The god has appeared" (abhūd devaḥ) [VaitS 16.15] and the verses beginning with "containing drops" (drapsavatyaḥ).
With these [verses], beginning with "That which the pressing-stone... (VaitS 24.1):
"That which the pressing-stone, moved by the arms, has squeezed from you, or that which the men have milked from your hands—may that swell for you, may that be restored for you, O King Soma."
O King Soma, whatever of your many well-formed and beloved limbs they have severed with the pressing-stone,
heal those with clarified butter and cause them to grow, so that we may dwell forever free from sin.

Whatever skin they have torn from you, whatever womb [they have entered], or if you have fallen from your place, or even if you are breathless—O Soma, this [restoration] has been prepared for us by you; O King, call us to our well-performed deeds!
Unite with out-breath and in-breath, and unite with sight and with hearing, O King Soma!
Whatever of yours is shattered, may all that be restored for you here; may he know us at the meeting-place of our paths.
Alas! The body, meeting with milk, becomes of another color;
to you, O Indu, we shall pay worship with an oblation; may we be masters of riches.
The ladles flow with clarified butter; they cause your limbs and joints to grow.
To you, O Soma, be homage and the cry of *vaṣaṭ*; and do you, O King, summon us to the performance of good deeds.
Having placed down the black antelope skin, he sprinkles it thoroughly with water.
(3.14.3) (24.3) Beginning with "With hymns to the waters" (*apāṃ sūktaiḥ*), they perform the ritual up to the ceremonial touching (*upasparśana*).
(3.14.4) (24.4) With the verse "Upward we [ascend]" (*ud vayaṃ*), they step upward. (3.14.5) (24.5)
They return, reciting: "We have drunk Soma" (Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad 3; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.2.4.5) and "We have gone to heaven" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 16.9.3). (3.14.6) (24.6)
With the verse, "The divine waters" (RV 7.89.1),
they worship the Āhavanīya fire.
(3.14.7) (24.7) Beginning with "I release" (*vimuñcāmi*) and ending with the ritual purification (*mārjana*), as prescribed in KauśS 6.11–13.
(3.14.8) (24.8) The *udayanīyā* offering is like the *prāyaṇīyā*;
one-fourth is for *pathyā svasti*.
(3.14.9) (24.9) The final conclusion.
While the Anūbandhyā cow stands facing the west, he pays homage according to his desire with the mantra: "O slayer of rivals" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 9.2.1).
If there is a set of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), then after the cleansing of the omentum (*vapāmārjana*), there is an animal sacrifice for Tvaṣṭṛ.

(6.4.12) (34.12) At a sacred bathing place, one should address a king or another person with the verse:
"These vital points of yours... (7.118).
(6.4.13) (34.13) He consecrates it with the mantra: "Saṃnaddham indro jayāti" (6.98).
(6.4.14) (34.14) He causes the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) to be brought for him when he is fully equipped.
A Brāhmaṇa causes him to accept it.
(6.4.15) (34.15) "O Lord of the Forest, with strong limbs... (*vanaspate vīḍvaṅgaḥ*, Ṛgveda 6.125).
Having thus consecrated the chariot, he causes [the sacrificer] to mount it.

With the verse, "Once released, fly away" (AVŚ 3.19.8), he releases the fourth arrow that has been discharged.
(6.4.18) (34.18) When he takes the Brahmin’s wealth, then the sacrificer redeems it.
(6.4.19) (34.19) “The buffalo at the Trikadruka rites” (RV 20.95.1);
“Forward for him the chariot-lead” (RV 20.95.2).
Thus are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses. (6.4.20) (34.20) With the verse,
"Drink of this strong, invigorating [soma]," he inserts twenty-four [verses].
(6.4.21) (34.21) Now, one who is in haste should perform the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, which serves as a ransom for the self, with a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā, and which is the "Pṛṣṭha-appeaser."
(6.5.1) (35.1) He recites the praise according to the hymn.
(6.5.2) (35.2) One should chant the stoma with one or two [verses],
but not before the twelfth [verse].
(6.5.3) (35.3) And also in the insertion of the *stotriya* verses during the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*).
(6.5.4) (35.4) At the two subsequent pressings, [the verses] are unlimited in number.
(6.5.5) (35.5) An *anurūpa* is one that corresponds to the *chandas* and the deity.
(6.5.6) (35.6) When there is no *prajñāna*, the *stotriya* is recited twice.
(6.5.7) (35.7) In the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*), the insertion (*āvāpa*) occurs after the *anurūpa* verse.
(6.5.8) (35.8) [One recites] the *pragāthas* during the midday [libation].
(6.5.9) (35.9) For the *ārambhaṇīyā* of the year-long sacrifice,
the *śvaḥstotriya* and *anurūpa* are: (6.5.10) (35.10) "indraṃ vo viśvatas pari" [RV 20.39.1].
Thus ends the *ārambhaṇīyā*.
(6.5.11) (35.11) “He has extended across the intermediate space” (20.39.2–5) is the *paryāsa*.
(6.5.12) (35.12) At the midday [pressing],
the *sāmapragātha* ending in a *kadvat* verse is "kan navyo atasīnām" [20.50]. (6.5.13) (35.13)
"With the Brahman, I yoke you, who are yoked by the Brahman"— this is the introductory verse.
(6.5.14) (35.14) We shall now explain the *stomas* for the purpose of exceeding [the standard number].
In the kingdom of the cow, there is the *trivṛt*;
for life, the *pañcadaśa*;
and on both [the back and the chest], the *saptadaśa*.
(6.5.16) (35.16) In the Uktha [sacrifice], there is the twenty-onefold [stoma].
In the Pṛṣṭhya [rite], there are the ninefold, fifteenfold, seventeenfold, twenty-onefold, twenty-sevenfold, and thirty-threefold [stomas].

In the kingdom [of the sacrifice], there are the Abhijit and Viśvajit; the fifteenfold and twenty-onefold [stomas] are used, and for the *pṛṣṭha* [laud], the twenty-sevenfold and thirty-threefold [stomas].
(6.5.18) (35.18) Among the Svarasāman chants, there is the seventeenfold [stoma].
(6.5.19) (35.19) At the Viṣuvat day, there is the twenty-one-fold [stoma].
(6.5.20) (35.20) In the *chandoma* days, there are the twenty-four-fold, the forty-four-fold, and the forty-eight-fold [stomas].
(6.5.21) (35.21) In the tenth [day], the twenty-one-fold [stoma] is used for both the Ājya and Pṛṣṭha [stotras].
(6.5.22) (35.22) At the Mahāvrata, there is the Pañcaviṃśa [Stoma].
(6.5.23) (35.23) In all cases, the *saṃsthā*, the *stoma*, and the *stotriya* are based upon the Sāmaveda; they are based upon the Sāmaveda.
(7.1.1) (36.1) Now follows the Rājasūya.
(7.1.2) (36.2) Before the full moon of Taiṣya, there is the Pavitra.
(7.1.3) (36.3) In the intervals between the months, there are ten *saṃsṛp* offerings.
(7.1.4) (36.4) On the full moon day of Māgha, the Abhiṣecanīya [sacrifice] takes place.
(7.1.5) (36.5) After the Marutvatīya [offering], there is the Bārhaspatya sacrifice.

(7.1.6–7) (36.6–7) To the east of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, he causes [the sacrificer] to mount and consecrates him upon a throne-seat (*āsandi*) covered with a tiger skin, with the mantra: "Become one among beings" (*bhūto bhūteṣu*).
(7.1.8) (36.8) On the full moon day of Phālguna, the Daśapeya sacrifice is performed.
(7.1.9) (36.9) The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are performed annually.
(7.1.10) (36.10) When [the fires] have been extinguished, on the full moon day of Caitra, the Pratyavarohaṇīya rite is to be performed.
(7.1.11) (36.11) On the two days following the full moon of Vaiśākha, there is prosperity.
(7.1.12) (36.12) From Jyaiṣṭhī comes Kṣatradhṛti.
(7.1.13) (36.13) From the full moon of Āṣāḍha, the purifier is for the sake of completion.
(7.1.14) (36.14) Now follows the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
(7.1.15) (36.15) On the full moon day of Phālguna, he gives the *brahmaudana* rice porridge to the Udgātṛ and his three assistants.
(7.1.16) (36.16) When the morning oblation has been offered, [he gives] a boon to the Brahmin.
(7.1.17) (36.17) The sacrifice to Agni and that to Pūṣan.
(7.1.18) (36.18) He consecrates with the mantra, "Become one who has the speed of the wind" (6.9.2), the horse as it is being harnessed. (7.1.19) (36.19)
[He recites] "Abhi tvā jarimāhita" (3.11.8) as he is being unyoked.
(7.1.20) (36.20) It was abandoned by Āśāpālīya.
(7.1.21) (36.21) For one year, there are three Sāvitrī sacrifices.
(7.1.22) (36.22) For the purpose of reciting the *pāriplava* narratives, they sit upon golden seats to the south of the sacrificial altar (*vedi*).
(7.1.23) (36.23) A rug and a cushion belong to the Brahman priest;
a seat-grass mat belongs to the sacrificer.
(7.1.24) (36.24) In the case of the Ākhyāna texts, he causes him to recite the Vyāhṛtis according to the respective Veda.
(7.1.25) (36.25) The initiation takes place at the end of the year;
there are twenty-one days of initiation.
(7.1.26) (36.26) The first day is like the first [day] of the *abhiplava* [six-day period];
the second is like the fourth [day] of the *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day period].
(7.1.27) (36.27) He consecrates with a mantra the horse being harnessed after the *bahiṣpavamāna* [laud]:
"May the Gandharvas and the waters of the two rivers harness you together for the sake of the year-long session;
to those who always protect you with vigilance, may Savitṛ grant them long life—be a guardian! (7.1.28) (36.28)
With the verse, "The divine Gandharva" (RV 10.85.21),
the Kauśika priest,
having seated the consecrated queen, covers her with an upper garment.
The sacrificer addresses those two [the wife and the Adhvaryu] with the verse:
"Cover yourselves with the heavenly world; place the vulva between your thighs; bring hither the ointment which is the living man's enjoyment for women. (VSM 23.20 + TS 7.4.19.1).
(7.1.31) (36.31) Because of the Hotṛ’s provocation, the Brahman priest [should address] the favorite wife [with the verse]:
"May he lift her up, as one carrying a load upon a mountain;
then let her waist swell, like one purifying herself in a cold wind" (VSM 23.26–27). (7.1.32) (36.32)
"Upwards him!"—
thus the attendants [address] the Brahman priest.
(7.1.33) (36.33) In the assembly, after the *brahmodya* (theological debate) between the *hotṛ* and the *adhvaryu*, the *brahman* priest questions the *udgātṛ*:

(7.2.1) (37.1) "I ask you for the sake of knowledge, O friend of the gods: if you have gone there with your mind, in which three steps of Viṣṇu, the victorious one, has this entire world entered? (VSM 23.49).
In response to that question, he said:
"The Person entered into the five; they were placed within the Person.
Reflecting upon this here, I am not your superior in the sacrifice, O priest. (VSM 23.52)
"You are neither superior nor inferior to me, nor am I prior to you; why then, O wise one, do you deign to speak such words as these which ought to be learned? You shall not become my equal."
(7.2.3) (37.3) Having all gone forth, they ask the sacrificer:
"I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth" (ŚB 9.10.13). [He replies:
"This is the altar" (ŚB 9.10.14).
Thus says the sacrificer.
(7.2.4) (37.4) In the third [day], there are two pressings, like those of the twenty-four-fold [stoma].
(7.2.5) (37.5) In the archetypal [sacrifice], the *ājyastotriya* and the *anurūpa* [verses] are those belonging to the archetype.
(7.2.6) (37.6) From the beginning of the third pressing, it is like the Atirātra sacrifice.
(7.2.7) (37.7) When the sacrifice is completed, there is a sacrificial post with two branches for five animals.

(7.2.10) (37.10) The human sacrifice is like the horse sacrifice.

thus thinks the sacrificer.

And being liberated by those [powers] that cause arousal.
(7.2.24) (37.24) The *śāmitra* fire being carried by female deer;

at the methane [offering], the Brahman priest [recites] "And the ponds with good drinking water...
(*suprapāṇā ca veśantā* [PS 20.128.9]).
(7.3.2) (38.2) The attendants follow from the east.

Thus say all [this being unattested elsewhere].

"The cows of the nobleman have eaten the barley, released in droves; I saw them wandering together with their herdsman.
Crying out, the nobleman’s men gathered around from all sides; how much will the master choose to bestow upon them? (RV 10.27.8).
Thus [he addresses] the Udgātṛ.

"Which of the two releases the bolt against him—the one who carries it or the one who would choose it? (RV 10.27.11).

"For we invoke you indeed" (RV 10.98).

3) and "ā no viśvāsu havya indraḥ" (RV 20.104.3–4) [are recited].

"The hero who overcomes all hostile armies" (RV 10.54.2),
and "For thus you are one who desires heroes" (RV 10.60.6).

In the second [set of days],...

(8.4.11) (42.11) The rites lasting for a year are explained by means of the Gavāmayana.
(8.4.12) (42.12) From this very [source] come the Ahīnas, the Rātrisattras,
and some Ekāhas as well.
(8.4.13) (42.13) In all cases, the arrangement of the desires is according to the Sāmaveda.
(8.4.14) (42.14) The *ahīna* sacrifices last from two days up to twelve days; they have an *atirātra* on either side.
(8.4.15) (42.15) The Rātrisattras beginning with the twelve-day sacrifice extend as far as one year.
(8.4.16) (42.16) The ten-night sacrifice has an Atirātra at both ends.
(8.4.17) (42.17) The twelve-day rite preceded by an Agniṣṭoma is an Ahīna sacrifice.
(8.4.18) (42.18) The sacrificial sessions (*ayana*) extend for as long as a thousand years. One should sacrifice with the *Viśvajit*, which is the counterpart of a thousand-year session.
(8.5.1) (43.1) The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) should take place in spring for a Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
in summer for a Rājanya desiring splendor (*tejas*);
and in the rainy season for a Vaiśya desiring prosperity (*puṣṭi*).
In autumn, for the removal of all diseases of everyone.
(8.5.2) (43.2) Some say that [the ritual] ends with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
"Of those who follow the Agnihotra," says Yuvan Kauśika.
(8.5.4) (43.4) For them, [the offering] of the new grain is in the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
(8.5.5) (43.5) The Agnihotra is performed with cooked rice from a pot or with barley gruel.
(8.5.6) (43.6) In the absence [of milk], having fed a cow fresh grass, one should [perform the rite] with her milk.
(8.5.7) (43.7) For one who desires prosperity, there should always be a vigil for the sacred fires.
(8.5.8) (43.8) The Agnihotra is for one who desires heaven.
(8.5.9) (43.9) With milk, [one attains] all desires.
(8.5.10) (43.10) For one who desires sensory power, [he should sacrifice] with curd.
(8.5.11) (43.11) For one desiring splendor, [he should sacrifice] with clarified butter.
(8.5.12) (43.12) For one desiring prosperity, [the oblation] should be with oil.
(8.5.13) (43.13) With boiled rice, [one should sacrifice] for one desiring offspring.
(8.5.14) (43.14) For one desiring a village, [he should offer] barley-gruel.
(8.5.15) (43.15) For one desiring strength, [the offering should be made] with rice grains.
(8.5.16) (43.16) [One should sacrifice] with Soma for one who desires spiritual luster.
(8.5.17) (43.17) For one desiring nourishment, [it should be offered] with meat.
(8.5.18) (43.18) [The rite] with water for one who desires long life.
(8.5.19) (43.19) The New and Full Moon sacrifices are for one who desires all things.
(8.5.20) (43.20) The Dākṣāyaṇayajña is for one desiring offspring.
(8.5.21) (43.21) The Sākaṃprasthāyya sacrifice is for one who desires cattle.
The Saṃkrama sacrifice is for one who desires all things.
(8.5.23) (43.23) For one desiring cattle, [the offering] is preceded by the *iḍā*.
(8.5.24) (43.24) The Sārvasenīya sacrifice is for one who desires offspring.
(8.5.25) (43.25) The Śaunakayajña is for one who desires the performance of malevolent magic.
(8.5.26) (43.26) The sacrifice of Vasiṣṭha for one desiring progeny.
(8.5.27) (43.27) The path of heaven and earth is for one who desires a firm foundation.
(8.5.28) (43.28) These are the sacrifices of the New and Full Moon and so forth.
(8.5.29) (43.29) The Āgrayaṇa [offering] is for one who desires food.
(8.5.30) (43.30) The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are for one who desires all things.
(8.5.31) (43.31) An animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra and Agni is for one who desires long life, progeny, and cattle.
The *yāma*, *śukaharī*, and *śuṇṭha* [mantras] are for one who desires freedom from disease and for one who desires the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*).
The horse of Tvaṣṭṛ belongs to one desiring offspring.
(8.5.34) (43.34) These two are performed for the sake of specific desires.
(8.5.35) (43.35) The *sutyā* rites are for one who desires all things.
(8.5.36) (43.36) The Ukthya [sacrifice] is for one who desires cattle.
(8.5.37) (43.37) The Vājapeya [is prescribed] for one who desires self-sovereignty.
(8.5.38) (43.38) The Atirātra [sacrifice] is for one who desires prosperity.
(8.5.39) (43.39) The Gavāmayana and the Dvādaśāha.
(8.5.40) (43.40) The Rājasūya is for one who desires sovereign rule.
(8.5.41) (43.41) The horse sacrifice and the human sacrifice are for one who desires all things.
(8.5.42) (43.42) The Sarvamedha is for one who desires preeminence.
(8.5.43) (43.43) Because desires are infinite, sacrifices are immeasurable.
(8.5.44) (43.44) These are explained by their respective *prakṛtis*.
(8.5.45) (43.45) The sequence of the sacrifice [is learned] from the Brāhmaṇa, as is the mending of what is torn.
He who studies these two Kalpas and he who knows them thus—by him all sacrifices have been performed, and he attains all desires.
